intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

units.title: Tectonic Forces
units.intro:
The Earth’s outer shell (the lithosphere) is broken into rigid **plates** that creep on the softer asthenosphere. Almost every large mountain, rift, volcano chain and earthquake belt sits on a plate edge. Internal heat drives the motion; we only see the results at the surface.

There are three relative motions. Name the motion first, then the landform — that is the safe exam pattern.

cards.title: 1.1 Tectonic Plates
body: The earth consists of a rigid outer layer called the lithosphere.
About 250 million years ago, there was a single super continent called Pangaea surrounded by a single super ocean known as Panthalassa.
About 210 million years ago Pangaea split into two land masses called Gondwanaland and Laurasia.

The splitting continued and in the northern hemisphere Laurasia split into North America and Eurasia (Europe and Asia) while in the southern hemisphere Gondwanaland broke into Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, Australia, New Zealand and Madagascar.
Subsequently, India separated from the Gondwanaland, moved further away and crashed into Asia.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Who proposed the Continental Drift theory in 1912?

steps.text: Alfred Wegener was a German meteorologist who formally proposed the Continental Drift theory in 1912, arguing that all continents were once part of a single supercontinent.
Harry Hess proposed Sea Floor Spreading in the 1960s.
Charles Richter developed the earthquake magnitude scale.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What was the single supercontinent that existed about $$250\text{ million years}$$ ago called?

steps.text: Pangaea is the name given to the giant supercontinent that incorporated almost all of Earth's landmasses before drifting apart.
Laurasia and Gondwanaland were the two fragments formed when Pangaea split.
Panthalassa was the giant ocean surrounding Pangaea.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The rigid outer layer of the Earth consisting of the crust and upper mantle is known as the:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Core definition**
The lithosphere is the rigid, outermost shell of Earth, comprising the crust and the solid, uppermost portion of the mantle. It is fractured into tectonic plates.

**Step 2: Contrast with asthenosphere**
The asthenosphere lies directly beneath the lithosphere and is semi-fluid/ductile, allowing the lithosphere to glide over it.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is **Lithosphere**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following landmasses was part of Gondwanaland after Pangaea split?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze split components**
When Pangaea split, Laurasia moved north and Gondwanaland moved south.

**Step 2: Identify components of Gondwanaland**
Gondwanaland included Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, Australia, and Madagascar.

**Step 3: Compare with options**
North America, Europe, and Asia were parts of Laurasia. Africa was part of Gondwanaland.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The correct option is **Africa**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Who proposed the Continental Drift theory in 1912?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Historical context**
Alfred Wegener was a German meteorologist who formally proposed the Continental Drift theory in 1912, arguing that all continents were once part of a single supercontinent.

**Step 2: Compare with other options**
Harry Hess proposed Sea Floor Spreading in the 1960s. Charles Richter developed the earthquake magnitude scale. Tuzo Wilson contributed to plate boundary theory.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct answer is **Alfred Wegener**.

cards.title: Plate tectonics: fuller notes
body: The Earth’s rigid outer layer (the **lithosphere**) is broken into large **plates** that move slowly over the softer **asthenosphere**, driven mainly by convection currents in the mantle. Plates move apart at **divergent** (constructive) boundaries, towards each other at **convergent** (destructive) boundaries, and slide past each other at **transform** boundaries. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries.

cards.title: Worked: weathering vs erosion
cards.problem: A granite boulder cracks in place after freeze–thaw. Is that weathering or erosion?

steps.text: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion moves the pieces.

cards.answer: Weathering (frost action). Erosion starts when water/wind/gravity carries fragments away.

cards.title: Divergent boundaries — plates pull apart
body: As two plates separate, magma rises and freezes into new crust. On a continent the crust first sags into a **rift valley** (East African Rift, the Afar / Danakil area). If rifting continues, the valley floods and becomes a narrow sea — that is the story of the **Red Sea**. In the open ocean the same process builds a mid-ocean ridge. Earthquakes here are usually shallow; volcanoes are common because the crust is thin.

cards.title: Convergent boundaries — plates meet
body: If one plate is oceanic, it is denser and **subducts** (dives) under the other. The diving slab melts; magma rises as a volcanic arc. A deep ocean trench marks the dive. If two continents meet, neither sinks easily — sediments crumple into **fold mountains** (think of a rug pushed across a floor). These collisions give the biggest ranges and deep earthquakes.

cards.title: Transform boundaries — plates slide past
body: Crust is neither created nor destroyed. Stress builds, then slips: earthquakes, offset rivers and fences, few volcanoes. Useful contrast question: “Why few volcanoes on a transform fault?” Because there is no melting slab and no gap for magma.

cards.title: Landforms built from inside
body:
- **Fold mountains** — compression wrinkles layered rock.
- **Block / fault mountains** — tension or shear snaps the crust; a block drops (graben) or is left standing (horst). Rift shoulders work this way.
- **Volcanoes** — magma reaches the surface at rifts and subduction zones.
- **Earthquakes** — sudden slip on a fault; energy travels as waves.

cards.title: Mnemonic — D.C.T.
body: Diverge = Divide (new crust, rift, Red Sea). Converge = Crash (trench or fold mountains). Transform = Slide (quakes, little lava). For Eritrea always add: “Our sea and Danakil sit on a divergent / rift setting.”

cards.title: How to write a tectonic paragraph
body: A 6-mark answer is usually: (1) name the boundary, (2) say what the plates do, (3) say what happens to crust / magma, (4) name the landform, (5) locate an example. Example: “The Red Sea is a divergent boundary. The African and Arabian plates are moving apart. Magma rises and new oceanic crust forms. The land first rifted, then flooded. That is why Eritrea has a young sea and a hot depression at Danakil.”

cards.title: How to write a tectonic paragraph
head: Feature
Typical boundary
Why
rows: Crust stretches and drops; magma fills the gap
Offset streams, strong quakes, little lava

cards.title: How to write a tectonic paragraph
body: Volcanoes are not random. They cluster at rifts (thin crust) and at subduction zones (melting slab). Hot spots (e.g. a plume under a plate) are the exception the book may mention only in passing — don’t spend the essay there unless asked.

Earthquakes: focus = underground slip point; epicentre = the place on the surface above it. Shallow quakes at rifts and transforms; a mix of depths at subduction. Damage depends on magnitude, depth, rock type and building quality — a geography paper still wants the plate cause first.

cards.q: What was the single supercontinent that existed about $$250\text{ million years}$$ ago called?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall definitions**
Pangaea is the name given to the giant supercontinent that incorporated almost all of Earth's landmasses before drifting apart.

**Step 2: Analyze other options**

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary driving mechanism responsible for the movement of tectonic plates?

options.A: Earth's gravitational pull from the moon

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand plate driving forces**
Tectonic plates are dragged by the lateral flow of mantle rock under thermal convection.

**Step 2: Identify convection mechanism**
Heat from the core causes hot rock in the mantle to rise, cool near the crust, spread horizontally, and sink, acting as a conveyor belt.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The driving mechanism is **Convection currents in the mantle**.

cards.problem: What is the primary driving mechanism responsible for the movement of tectonic plates?

steps.text: Tectonic plates are dragged by the lateral flow of mantle rock under thermal convection.
Heat from the core causes hot rock in the mantle to rise, cool near the crust, spread horizontally, and sink, acting as a conveyor belt.
The driving mechanism is **Convection currents in the mantle**.

cards.title: Worked: Red Sea
cards.problem: Red Sea is widening — boundary type?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which statement is **not true** about plate tectonics?

options.A: Sea floor spreading caused by the moving apart of plates at mid-oceanic ridges.
options.B: Movement of plates is caused by convection currents.
options.C: By the process of divergent boundaries a new crust is formed.
options.D: In subduction zone plates push one another.
options.E: Since 250 million years continents have been stopped from moving.

cards.why: Statement E is false because tectonic plates and continents are **constantly moving** (at a rate of a few centimeters per year) and have not stopped since the Earth formed. The other statements correctly describe plate movements and their effects.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A plate boundary formed when two plates move away from each other is called
cards.why: A divergent boundary (or constructive boundary) occurs when tectonic plates pull apart. This leads to rifting and the formation of new crust (e.g., the Red Sea Rift).

cards.title: 1.3 Folding
body: When plates move towards each other and collide, the compressive forces that are created make the rock layers bend up and down.
Subsequently, the shape of the resulting land form looks like corrugated iron.
The process of bending of layers of the earth’s crust is called **folding**, and the resultant land forms are known as folds.
Folding occurs in sedimentary rock layers because sedimentary rocks are soft rocks that bend easily.
Depending on the intensity and direction of the compressive forces applied to the rock layers, different types of folds are created.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of plate boundary is also referred to as a "constructive" boundary?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define boundary types**
A constructive boundary is one where new crustal material is created.

**Step 2: Examine divergent boundaries**
At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, and upwelling magma solidifies into new crust along the rift zone.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct answer is **Divergent boundary**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which type of plate boundary is also referred to as a "constructive" boundary?

steps.text: A constructive boundary is one where new crustal material is created.
At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, and upwelling magma solidifies into new crust along the rift zone.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The Andes Mountains in South America are a prime example of fold mountains formed by which type of plate convergence?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze geographic location**
The Andes are located along the western margin of South America where the Nazca oceanic plate collides with the South American continental plate.

**Step 2: Identify subduction/collision type**
Because the Nazca plate is oceanic and Nazca is denser, it subducts beneath the continental plate, causing folding, volcanic arcs, and mountain building.

**Step 3: Final Result**
This is **Oceanic-Continental convergence**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The Andes Mountains in South America are a prime example of fold mountains formed by which type of plate convergence?

steps.text: The Andes are located along the western margin of South America where the Nazca oceanic plate collides with the South American continental plate.
Because the Nazca plate is oceanic and Nazca is denser, it subducts beneath the continental plate, causing folding, volcanic arcs, and mountain building.

cards.title: Folding
body: **Compression** bends rock layers into folds. An upfold is an **anticline**; a downfold is a **syncline**. Strong compression makes overfolds and overthrust folds. Large-scale fold mountains such as the Alps, the Himalayas and the Atlas are called **fold mountains**. **Tension** pulls rocks apart and makes **faults**: a block dropped between two faults is a **rift valley** (like the Great Rift Valley that passes through the Danakil depression); a block raised between faults is a **horst** (block mountain).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Fold mountains are formed when ____.

options.A: compressional forces push layers of rock together so they bend
options.B: lava builds up around a vent
options.D: tensional forces pull the crust apart

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Folding happens at convergent plate boundaries.

**Step 2:** Compression makes rock layers bend into anticlines (up-folds) and synclines (down-folds).

**Step 3:** Tension forms faults and rift valleys; lava builds volcanoes.

**Tip:** Read the contour values first (do they rise or fall?), then the spacing (close = steep, wide = gentle) and the shape (V up = valley, V down = spur).

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)
body: - Fold mountains = compression; rift shoulders = fault blocks.

cards.title: 1.4.1 Normal fault
body: Normal fault is formed where there is tensional force.
The Rift valley and block mountains are examples of land forms formed where normal faults occur.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Reverse fault
body: A reverse fault is formed by compressional forces.
The weight of the portion of the raised block hanging over the other block can be so high that it can lead to a force that causes the block to break off.

cards.title: 1.4.3 Tear fault
body: In a tear fault, the block of the earth’s crust moves in a horizontal direction, one side sliding past the other along the fault line.
The existence of the tear fault can be observed when looking at a river.
In such a case, the river turns at right angle at the fault and flows along the fault line for a short distance before it turns to its original direction.
A tear fault does not have a fault scrap because no block is raised or slipped down.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is a classic example of a transform plate boundary?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define transform boundary**
A transform boundary is where plates slide horizontally past each other.

**Step 2: Match examples**
Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Great Rift Valley are divergent. The Himalayas are convergent. The San Andreas Fault is a strike-slip transform fault.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct example is **The San Andreas Fault**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following is a classic example of a transform plate boundary?

steps.text: A transform boundary is where plates slide horizontally past each other.
Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Great Rift Valley are divergent. The Himalayas are convergent. The San Andreas Fault is a strike-slip transform fault.
The correct example is **The San Andreas Fault**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a symmetrical fold, the upper arch-like fold is structurally called a/an:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify fold parts**
An anticline is an upward-arching fold of rock layers, shaped like an arch or 'A'.

**Step 2: Identify other parts**
A syncline is a downward trough-like fold. A monocline is a one-sided step fold. Limbs are the flanks of the fold.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The arch-like upfold is an **Anticline**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: In a symmetrical fold, the upper arch-like fold is structurally called a/an:

steps.text: An anticline is an upward-arching fold of rock layers, shaped like an arch or 'A'.
A syncline is a downward trough-like fold. A monocline is a one-sided step fold. Limbs are the flanks of the fold.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Rift valley and block mountains are good examples of _________ fault.
cards.why: Rift valleys and block mountains (horsts and grabens) are formed by tensional forces in the crust, which result in **normal faulting** where blocks of land subside or rise.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The majority of mountains in Africa are constructed through volcanic eruptions but Mount Ruwenzori was formed by the process of
cards.why: Mount Ruwenzori is a classic example of a 'Block Mountain' (Horst). It was formed by tectonic movements associated with the Great Rift Valley system, specifically through the process of faulting (where blocks of crust are pushed up between normal faults).

cards.title: 1.5.1 The damage earthquakes cause
body: The amount of damage caused by an earthquake depends on its magnitude.
The damage is worsened by the disruption of essential services like water and power supply, transport, and the damage caused by fire started by exposed electric wires and leakage from gas pipes.
One day in 2003 an earthquake struck before dawn and destroyed most of the ancient Silk Road of Bam.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Distribution of earthquakes in the world
body: Japan, Indonesia and the west coast of North and South America experience a number of severe earthquakes.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of fault is formed when tensional forces pull the crust apart, causing the hanging wall to slip downward?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand stress and faulting**
Tensional forces stretch and pull the crust, which leads to extension.

**Step 2: Identify the relative movement**
Under tension, gravity pulls the hanging wall down relative to the footwall, which is the defining movement of a normal fault.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct fault type is a **Normal fault**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which type of fault is formed when tensional forces pull the crust apart, causing the hanging wall to slip downward?

steps.text: Tensional forces stretch and pull the crust, which leads to extension.
Under tension, gravity pulls the hanging wall down relative to the footwall, which is the defining movement of a normal fault.
The correct fault type is a **Normal fault**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Mount Ruwenzori in East Africa is an example of a block mountain, structurally known as a:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall block mountain structures**
A block mountain is formed when a portion of the crust is uplifted between parallel normal faults.

**Step 2: Identify geological terms**
The raised block is called a horst, and the dropped trough is called a graben.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Mount Ruwenzori is a **Horst**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Mount Ruwenzori in East Africa is an example of a block mountain, structurally known as a:

steps.text: A block mountain is formed when a portion of the crust is uplifted between parallel normal faults.
The raised block is called a horst, and the dropped trough is called a graben.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The point on the earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake is the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The focus is the point underground where the rock breaks.

**Step 2:** The epicentre is directly above it on the surface.

**Step 3:** Shaking is usually strongest near the epicentre.

**Tip:** Read the contour values first (do they rise or fall?), then the spacing (close = steep, wide = gentle) and the shape (V up = valley, V down = spur).

cards.title: 1.6.1 What is a volcano?
body: **Volcanism** is the process by which magma (molten rock materials) moves through the cracks of the earth’s crust until it reaches the surface and solidifies to form hard rocks.
All volcanoes are thus formed by the accumulation of lava and are generally conical in shape.
The magma, which forms deep in the earth, erupts through vents or long cracks called fissures.
The rising magma does not reach the surface in a regular manner.

cards.title: 1.6.2 Types of volcanic activity
body: The major land forms formed by extrusive volcanic activities are composite cone, cinder cone and shield volcanoes as well as calderas and lava plateaus.
Composite volcanoes: Composite volcanoes are composed of explosively erupted fragmental materials covered with nonexplosively erupted lava flows and other volcanic materials.
Shield volcanoes (volcanic shields): are roundish, moundlike volcanoes with gentle slopes constructed mainly of many fluid basaltic lava flows that erupt nonexplosively.
Cinder cone: A cinder cone is a small volcanic mountain formed by the accumulation of mainly cinders (rock pieces) ejected during explosive volcanic eruptions.

cards.title: 1.6.3 Distribution of volcanoes
body: Most earthquakes also occur along these boundaries, an indication of the close connection between plate boundaries, earthquakes, and volcanic activities.
The main areas of volcanoes and earthquakes are the Pacific ring of fire, the Alpine-Himalayan Belt, and the Mid-Atlantic Oceanic Ridge.

cards.title: 1.6.4 Effects of volcanoes on humans
body: Volcanic activities have both negative and positive effects on peoples’ lives.
Volcanic ash clouds also disrupt air transport.

Yet their positive effects include the beautiful features produced are important sources of recreation and tourism, the fertile soil that results when the lava has weathered, and the production of geothermal energy from hot springs and geysers.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the underground origin of an earthquake is called the:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish earthquake points**
The underground point where rupture begins is the focus (or hypocenter).

**Step 2: Identify the surface point**
The point on the surface vertically above the focus is defined as the epicenter.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is **Epicenter**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the underground origin of an earthquake is called the:

steps.text: The underground point where rupture begins is the focus (or hypocenter).
The point on the surface vertically above the focus is defined as the epicenter.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What highly sensitive instrument is used by seismologists to detect and record seismic waves?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify instruments**
A seismograph is an instrument that detects and records earthquake-generated vibrations.

**Step 2: Discard other options**
A barometer measures air pressure. A thermometer measures temperature. An altimeter measures altitude.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct instrument is a **Seismograph**.

cards.problem: What highly sensitive instrument is used by seismologists to detect and record seismic waves?

steps.text: A seismograph is an instrument that detects and records earthquake-generated vibrations.
A barometer measures air pressure. A thermometer measures temperature. An altimeter measures altitude.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are landforms of extrusive volcanos except?
cards.why: **Extrusive** volcanic landforms are formed when magma reaches the Earth's surface (lava). Examples include Composite volcanoes, Calderas, and Cinder cones. **Intrusive** landforms are formed when magma cools inside the Earth's crust. A **Dyke** is an intrusive feature (a vertical sheet of rock).

glossary.meaning: Mountains formed when tension or compression makes the crust crack and a block is raised between faults (horst), e.g. Mount Ruwenzori.
Magma reaches the surface at rifts and subduction zones.
Sudden shaking of the ground caused by rocks slipping along a fault or by volcanic activity.
The epicenter is the place that suffers the highest damage of the earthquake.
The cracking of rocks in the earth's crust with movement of the blocks along the crack (fault).

tips.text: Hundreds of millions years ago there was a single continent. This single continent first split into two huge land masses - Laurasia and Gondwanaland.
Subsequently, these land masses further split to form the tectonic plates or crustal plates.
The tectonic plates are in constant motion due to the convection currents created by the magma in the mantle.
The boundaries along which the plates move are of three types. They are divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries.
In a divergent boundary, two palates move away from each other, while a convergent boundary is a boundary where two plates collide against each other.
A transform boundary is where two plates slide horizontally past one another.

The movements are the cause for the drifting of the continents as well as the formation of the fold mountains, different kinds of faults, rift valleys, block mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes along the plate boundaries.
This is why the location of the concentration of earthquakes, volcanoes and unstable areas of the world are the same.

questions.q: The German meteorologist who proposed the theory of **continental drift** in 1912 was:
why: **Alfred Wegener** proposed the Continental Drift theory in 1912, suggesting that all continents were once joined in a single supercontinent called **Pangaea** before drifting apart.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which one of the following is **not** part of Gondwanaland?
why: **Gondwanaland** was the southern supercontinent that included Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, India, and Madagascar. **Austria** was part of the northern supercontinent, **Laurasia**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In the splitting of the continents, which pair is in the wrong category?
why:
According to the Continental Drift theory, the supercontinent Pangea split into **Laurasia** (North) and **Gondwanaland** (South). 
- Gondwanaland included: Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, and Australia.
- Laurasia included: North America and Eurasia (Europe/Asia).
Pair C (Africa, Europe) is the 'wrong category' because Africa was part of Gondwanaland, while Europe was part of Laurasia.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Laurasia in the past was composed of much of the present day
why:
**Step 1:** Recall the theory of Continental Drift. Millions of years ago, the supercontinent Pangea split into two smaller supercontinents.
**Step 2:** Identify the two parts. The northern part was Laurasia, and the southern part was Gondwanaland.
**Step 3:** List the modern continents from Laurasia. It included North America, Europe, and Asia (collectively Eurasia).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Mountains formed by the bending of sedimentary rocks are called:
why: **Fold mountains** are formed when tectonic plates collide and push layers of sedimentary rock upward, causing them to bend and fold.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: There was a single super continent about 250 million years ago called:
why: **Pangaea** was a supercontinent that existed during the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras. It began to break apart about 200 million years ago into Laurasia and Gondwanaland.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The East African Rift system is found along the
why: The East African Rift is an active continental rift zone where the African Plate is splitting into two smaller plates (Somali and Nubian). This process occurs at a **divergent plate boundary**, where plates move away from each other.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Before the continents drifted to the current position, all of the following were joined with African plate, **except**
why: Africa was the center of the supercontinent Gondwanaland, which included South America, India, Arabia, Madagascar, Antarctica, and Australia. **North America** was part of the northern supercontinent, Laurasia.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In symmetric fold the valley of the mountain is called _____
why: In folding, the downward-arching fold (the valley part) is called a **syncline**, while the upward-arching fold (the crest) is called an anticline.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: **Collision** of two continental crust form:
why: When two continental plates collide, neither is subducted because they have similar densities. Instead, the crust thickens and is forced upward, forming massive fold mountains like the **Himalayas** and high-altitude regions like the **Tibetan Plateau**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.
